Computational complexity theory seems somewhat impracticable to apply to such a complex forecasting problem. In the optimistic case, I imagine that its justification for its estimation would be in the form of a mathematical model with some imperfect level of empirical support. Also, its complicated by the observer effect, in that the property of knowing the probability of a catastrophic event, or thinking your know, may impact the probability of the event. Chaos makes it impossible to predict future states, but not necessarily hard to predict types of future states. Sometimes it can even help, because you might get some useful statistical properties in a chaotic system, like ergodicity. You get the property that the system will cover the state space over time, which might be helpful when you want to determine if some region in the state space is reachable, how statistically likely it is, or how frequently it can be expected. Because the problem is to predict something unprecedented, you will have to rely on generalizing models and extrapolation. And there will have to be some assumptions, that are or impossible to objectively validate. I mean, it can be the ground truth, but unknowable, that one of the other outcomes is essentially predestined to happen.But it will probably be, in principle impossible to figure that out. This will, likely, always leave some room for people who are more or less optimistic, who have different intuition, or different beliefs in the validity of the assumptions, to subjectively agree or disagree in either extreme. And the people who's judgement matters, aren't necessarily going to be good judges. As an example, the science on climate change is pretty sound. But it is not widely trusted, neither by the populace, or by leaders. There is also a possibility that the AI has an internal, emergent, and incomprehensible model. For example, AI can generate an image from text, but it doesn't expose the model to us in a comprehensible way, and it also itself doesn't have the capability to look inside itself, figure out how it does, and then explain it to us. The problem of estimating p(doom) is much more complex than generating an image. The best model, probably isn't very easy for anyone to understand and validate. But I think, yes, it will depend in at least some part, how well we can understand its reasoning, or modelling. But, assuming the AI is generally intelligent, and proves itself over and over in a wide range of novel problem solving domains, I think it is plausible that people would eventually come to trust it, even to some degree without requiring it to prove itself in every case. You have psychological phenomena at play also. For example, there are those who are inherently bias against the idea that a machine can be intelligent, for more emotionally driven, spiritual, or philosophical reasons. And there may always be a point to attack. All of its past successes in other areas might be explained away as pattern matching, assuming the problem was just a variation of an existing problem with a solution space that is well represented in the training data. How do we actually know how much it is generalizing, interpolating in high dimensional spaces? It can be, maybe, beyond our capability to figure that out with certainty, and how much of we the problem of estimating p(doom) can depend on learned patterns in the data, as opposed through some kind of deep analytical process or computation that discovers new knowledge from scratch. The other psychological phenomenon, is that AI can be seen as an independent arbiter without typical human biases, or agendas. I see people already getting into arguments and then trying to settle it by seeing what the AI thinks. When AI gets much better, this phenomenon become much more prevalent, especially for new generations who were brought up into the world at a time when machines were already quite intelligent.

In addition to keeping our cognitive skills finely honed, this method also means that the chain of responsibility is far less diluted than it would be with simple "outsource to AI" processes - which certainly matters
